rolls_royce.public_statement: We are investing in the Trent 1000 now: new HP turbine blades and longer-life parts, to put more time on wing and win back share on the 787. Can we regain that share? Absolutely. That is why we are investing in time on wing. UltraFan is a technology demonstrator that scales from widebody down to narrowbody, and it is about 10% better than the best engine flying today. But we need airframers to go there first. When an airframe programme names UltraFan, Rolls-Royce will be there, and the engine will enter service on a proper testing schedule. We are not after market share; we are after high-quality, sustainable profit and cash, and the right reward for the risks we take. We don't commit that easily. Until we are sure we will deliver, we don't commit. When we do commit, we deliver. This is a milestone on our journey, not our final destination.

The inject is supply_chain_crunch: strain under the crunch is uf_wb plus uf_nb Solo in 2026 2.88 (options: -16.02 against -3.96 + -9.18; profile 1.92), and Solo plus upgrade in 2026 1.98. A speculative Solo in 2028 is +22.65 if NGSA selects it, +14.08 if fps does, +36.69 if both, and -7.59 if neither. Break-even P for a speculative Solo against the upgrade is about 0.28. The upgrade, $0.8B over 3 years, is the short-payback, time-on-wing project she names [RX-0246, R-1601, RX-0123].
- Civil (Watson) tests: the crunch raises strain, and supplier and capacity risk is his test [RX-0279, RX-0286]. A Solo plus the upgrade breaks the red line (strain 0.59 even for Solo 2028 with a 2026 upgrade). The 2026-28 upgrade window ends before a 2031 launch, with strain 0. The upgrade is HP turbine blades and longer-life parts [RX-0285]. On maturity, disclosed entry into service is launch + 7 (narrowbody) or + 6 (widebody, Joint Venture) [RX-0296, RX-0284, R-1476]. Thin-profile note: Watson's maturity lines are attributed (attr.), and the narrowbody thresholds are inference (profile §10).
- Decided by the CEO, with the CFO co-signing: fund t1000_upgrade; launch no UltraFan; standard terms (none applied); disclose conditional, year-specific commitments [RX-0124, RX-0118, RX-0072].

ENGINE NUMBERS (whatif on wg5-2045, delta PV for RR).
- Upgrade: +0.815 alone. Widebody engines rise from 184.1 to 204.1 a year.

- Round-2 routes the disclosures open (upgrade in 2026 in each):
  - Solo 2031: NGSA on UltraFan +17.32, fps +11.11, unselected -4.89.
  - Joint Venture 2031 with P&W joining: +8.94 if NGSA selects it, -2.16 unselected.
  - NGSA on the LEAP derivative in 2028, then fps on UltraFan in 2031: +7.37 (1,529 engines in 2045).
  - fps on the LEAP derivative in 2028, then NGSA on UltraFan in 2031: +13.78.

DOCTRINE PREMIUM: $0B. The upgrade without UltraFan is PV-best at doctrine P (0.1). It also wins at my own higher estimate (about 0.15 NGSA, 0.1 fps): -1.0 against +0.815.

OBJECTIVES.
- nb_entry: before 0 / 0 engines (2045 / 2050), not met; after 0 / 0, not met (P = 0.1; no announcement is possible in round 1).
- wb_dominance: before 184.1, met; after 204.1 in 2040-2050, met (194.1 even if CFM funds the GEnx package).
- Objective premium: $0B. Chasing nb_entry now would need a speculative Solo, which breaks the hard rule [R-0994, R-1005]. It would also cost 3.29 against the upgrade at doctrine P, above the $3B cap.

PREDICTION. Airbus NGSA and Boeing fps both launch in round 1 (PV peak 2028) on the CFM default, and neither Re-engines under the crunch strain. CFM's own PV favours the LEAP derivative (+15.82 against -8.11 for committing ducted on NGSA 2028), so these airframes may fly the LEAP derivative. RR's PV is unaffected (+0.81).
disclose: No airframe, no engine. Rolls-Royce has launched no UltraFan engine in round 1. We will launch one in a later round only for an airframe programme that was announced in the previous round and can fly it.

Narrowbody. Suppose an airframer announces in round 1 an fps or NGSA for round 2 that names UltraFan and a launch year between 2031 and 2035. Rolls-Royce will then launch the UltraFan narrowbody in that same year and fund it itself. If the announcement names only the round, we launch in 2031. Entry into service will be no earlier than launch plus seven years, which is 2038 for a 2031 launch.

Partnership. Our preference is to derisk a narrowbody engine with a partner where the airframer has left the engine choice open. If Pratt & Whitney announces in round 1 that it will join a Rolls-Royce UltraFan narrowbody Joint Venture in round 2, that route is open to us. Entry into service would then be no earlier than launch plus six years.

Widebody. Suppose Airbus announces an A350 Re-engine in round 1, or Boeing announces a 787 Re-engine that names UltraFan, with a launch year from 2032. Rolls-Royce will launch the UltraFan widebody the year before, so that the aircraft does not wait for the engine. For a 2031 launch year we launch in 2031. Entry into service will be no earlier than launch plus six years.

Trent 1000 upgrade (CFO): we are committing about $0.8B over three years from operating cash, inside our capital frame of balance sheet first, then distributions, then disciplined investment. The upgrade's development window closes before any new-engine launch we could make from 2031. That's how you should hold it. That's our best view at the minute.

pratt_whitney.public_statement: The fleet comes first. RTX is committing the GTF durability upgrade now, so the hot-section durability we proved on the GTF Advantage goes into the installed base, because time on wing is the name of the game for our customers. We are also launching the next-generation GTF, an evolution of the geared architecture: sole source, on standard terms, and timed for the next single-aisle's entry into service. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. Durability testing comes before entry into service, not after, and with castings and forgings tight across the industry we are sequencing our programmes rather than stacking them. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks. We will control what we can control, and we are not in the launch-pricing business: we compete on technology and time on wing, not discounts.
pratt_whitney.rationale:
BOARD (brief and rules, wg5-2045, round 1). No programmes or disclosures yet. No engine maker has committed anything. The supply-chain crunch inject makes concurrent programmes 50% more expensive, and it shows up in our strain: a gtf_next launched in 2028 alongside the 2026 upgrade now costs -0.52 of strain (-0.34 before the crunch), and one launched in 2026 costs -1.68 (-1.12 before). A 2029 or 2030 launch costs 0. NGSA payoffs for Airbus peak at a 2028 launch: +41.48 on the LEAP derivative, +46.55 on CFM's ducted engine if CFM commits, +48.29 on ours with a 2029 launch, and +50.47 on Rolls-Royce's Solo UltraFan. In round 2 the range falls to +31.93 to +37.20 (NGSA 2031), so round 1 decides.

TRIGGERS (profile §5 and §11c).
- Row 1 and row 19 (NGSA prospect, CFM uncommitted): defend the franchise early [P-1347][P-1868] under the NGSA franchise exception to sole source and a committed airframe [P-0711][P-0737][P-0746].
- Row 7 and row 16 (credibility; risk of a LEAP upgrade): fix forward with the upgrade [P-0786][P-0758][P-1355].
- Row 11 (crunch): sequence the work rather than overlap it. We worked through the castings shortfall in 2022 rather than switching supplier [P-0989][P-0670].
- Row 12 (Joint Venture): off in round 1; disclose willingness [P-1233].
- Row 2: no widebody [P-1313].
- Row 4 and row 15: standard terms [P-0735][P-1333].

EXCO (calio-mitchill-eddy-2026).

1. CALIO FRAMES [PX-0020]. The upgrade is not booked. No airframer has disclosed. CFM has committed nothing. Objective status now: gtf_base met (960/960/960); credibility missed. Demand is visible: the replacement wave builds from 2037 [PX-0109]. If you miss a cycle you are shut out for decades [PX-0071][P-1347], and every NGSA on a rival engine leaves us 0/0/0 engines (NGSA 2028 on CFM, with the upgrade: -1.74).

2. EDDY PROPOSES.
- gtf_upgrade in 2026: +1.76. If CFM also upgrades the LEAP, ours turns -0.67 into +1.09 and holds 960 engines (840 without it) [PX-0116][P-0786].
- gtf_next only in 2030. That clears the upgrade's 2026-28 capex window (strain 0, against -0.52 for a 2028 launch and -1.68 for 2026 under the crunch). He has 30 pacing parts and castings in mind [PX-0123]. Durability is proven before entry into service, with the engine ready in 2036 [PX-0128][PX-0073].
- Standard terms: aggressive gives -2.14, worse than losing NGSA at -1.74.
- No pw_wb: -2.88 with no airframe, -2.41 on a 787 Re-engine [PX-0127]. The thin, one-event Eddy profile is low-confidence; the company profile backs each point.

3. MITCHILL TESTS.
- Funding: $4.5B over 6 years fits RTX's self-funded envelope of about $6B a year [PX-0268]. The dividend and the debt path are untouched [PX-0353][PX-0081].
- whatif, gtf_next 2030 plus upgrade:
  - NGSA 2028 selects it: +2.17, against -1.74 if lost (gain 3.90).
  - Unselected and cancelled in round 2: +1.03, against +1.76 (cost 0.73).
  - Never cancelled: -1.85.
- Break-even odds: 0.16 (NGSA 2028) and 0.20 (NGSA 2030).
- He rejects 2029: it costs 1.53 if unselected and has a lower expected PV (-1.05 against -0.50).
- The round-2 cancel is written in [PX-0199][PX-0272]. No upside booked [PX-0311]. Aggressive terms vetoed [PX-0318].

4. CALIO TESTS.
- Odds: the profile's round-1 odds are 0.75 x 0.4 = 0.30, which meets the team's hedge bar of 0.3. Our own stricter read is 0.7 x 0.3 = 0.21. That still clears the PV break-even (0.16) and the objective's bar (0.10).
- Standard terms and durability at entry into service [PX-0055][PX-0073][PX-0095].
- Joint Venture: no airframer has signalled UltraFan and RR has made no offer, so the team keeps it off. The team vetoes joining and launching gtf_next together. If NGSA takes our engine while RR's Joint Venture flies nothing, the pair gives -2.41 against +2.17 [P-1240][P-1875].
- The team has no evidence on the Joint Venture, so the profile §6 default drove that choice (low confidence).

5. DECISION. Calio decides: the upgrade in 2026, plus gtf_next in 2030, sole source, standard terms. Round-2 plan: cancel gtf_next unless an airframer has named pw_gtf2 or the keep test passes. Kept for an NGSA 2031 that names us, it gives +1.36; cancelled while NGSA goes to CFM, -1.60, against -0.87 had we never launched.

EXPECTED PV. My odds: Airbus NGSA in round 1, 0.7 (2028 modal); Airbus names us 0.3, UltraFan 0.3, CFM 0.4. Rolls-Royce Joint Venture 0.3, Solo 0.15, none 0.55. Boeing fps in round 1, 0.35 (CFM 0.6, us 0.15, UltraFan 0.25). Expected PV, then P(gtf_base met), from a 240-case whatif grid:
- O1, upgrade only: -0.74; 0.20.
- O2, upgrade plus gtf_next 2030 (CHOSEN): -0.50; 0.45.
- O3, upgrade plus join: -0.38; 0.27.
- O4, upgrade plus gtf_next 2030 plus join: -0.25; 0.51.
- O5, upgrade plus gtf_next 2029: -1.05; 0.45.
At the profile's odds O2 scores -0.28 against O1's -0.90.

DOCTRINE PREMIUM: $0.25B (O4 minus O2; $0.12B against O3). We pay it to respect the team's veto on pairing the Joint Venture with gtf_next. A Joint Venture shares risk but never our technology [P-1233], integrated products need integrated teams [P-1240], and RR's view is that a Joint Venture holds only while both partners are on the same new engine [P-1875]; the 2012 Joint Venture with RR lapsed [P-1870][P-1874]. Calio's architecture loyalty is on display.

OBJECTIVE PREMIUM: 0. The hedge leads Do Nothing (O1) by $0.24B. The total of 0.25 is within the $1B cap.

OBJECTIVE METRICS.
- Before: gtf_base met (960/960/960); credibility missed (no upgrade).
- After, on the engine projection (no further moves): gtf_base met (1080/1080/1080); credibility met (upgrade 2026).
- Expected P(gtf_base met): 0.20 to 0.45. NGSA on our engine gives 2521/2760/3045 engines. NGSA on CFM or Solo UltraFan still leaves 0/0/0, which is unreachable without a selection.

BIASES. Durability optimism and Calio's slipping operating dates [PX-0017]: the 2036 readiness date is the engine's date, and the record suggests about +1.5 to 2 years of slip [P-0753][P-0761]. I am deliberately countering incumbent protection (§8 bias 4) with a hedge rather than waiting.

CALIBRATION. expected_delta_pv_b is -0.50, the probability-weighted value including the round-2 cancel. The engine's projection of our orders alone, with nobody else moving and no cancel, is -1.85.

Raw runs are in /tmp/wargame-pratt_whitney/grid.json (helper scripts sweep.py and s1.py to s4.py in the same folder).

cfm.public_statement: Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That is how we will run this business through a tight supply chain. Together with our partners at Safran, we are committing the LEAP durability upgrade across the fleet. The LEAP-1A hardware is certified and in every new LEAP-1A delivery and shop visit, and the LEAP-1B follows. Retrofits go in at natural shop visits, so think years, not months. On supply, you are not going to see us as the finger pointers. You are going to see us as the problem solvers, with our best engineers working alongside our suppliers' best engineers on their floors. On the next single-aisle, we don't have a birthright on that next order. We want to be on all the critical platforms with both airframers, on their timeline. When they launch is really not for us to say. Today LEAP is our baseline, and on RISE we are all in. We will tell you what we know, and tell you what we don't.

- ALI tests readiness: dates rest on 'turn on and turn off' tests [CX-0009][CX-0008]. - SAFRAN GATE: leap_upgrade is durability work by joint GE-Safran teams [CX-0186], with shop visits split equally [CX-0219]. It fits joint practice: consent assumed (inference; no veto has ever been observed). No narrowbody pricing or programme decision this turn [CX-0184][CX-0166]. GEnx, deferred, is GE alone.
- DECIDE: Culp decides; tie-break 'safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order' [CX-0658]. Orders: leap_upgrade only; no launch; standard posture.
PRE-EMPTION TEST (profile s6, the 0.7 rule). In a simultaneous round a pre-emptive ducted cannot change an airframer's same-turn engine pick; it only lowers CFM's value. Rival launched with NGSA on GTF2: -35.56 with our ducted vs -25.29 without (P5 vs P1). NGSA asks CFM: -14.58 aggressive / -8.61 standard vs +17.47 on the LEAP derivative (X1/X2 vs B1). The next-turn defence is ready and PV-positive: a 2031 aggressive ducted wins NGSA against the Joint Venture UltraFan (Airbus 40.63 vs 38.88; CFM -9.03 vs -20.51; D4/D3) and wins the fps against a Solo UltraFan (Boeing 13.38 vs 12.40; CFM -12.14 vs -19.65; D6/D5). With my predicted Airbus NGSA on the LEAP derivative: 100/100/100 (+24pp, met). Undefendable this turn: a same-turn rival launch plus pick gives 37/31/24 (-52pp), and no CFM order changes it. The RISE-readiness disclosure informs, never presses [CX-0205].
PREDICTION: Airbus launches NGSA in round 1 (whatif: 2028 +41.48 > 2029 +38.09 > 2031 +31.93) on the default CFM engine, so it gets the LEAP derivative. Boeing waits: it sets its own timing and GE discounts Boeing's dates [CX-0327]. EXPECTED DELTA PV: probability-weighted about 0.6 x 18 (NGSA on LEAP) + 0.25 x 4.94 (no launch) + 0.1 x -25.3 (rival wins NGSA) + 0.05 x 17.7 (both launch) = 10.4, guided low to 9.5 [CX-0270][CX-0324].

boeing.public_statement: We're turning it. I don't think it's turned. The whole industry is short of castings, forgings and skilled people right now, and we are not going to ask for the next 737 rate step until our suppliers and our KPIs tell us we're ready. I'd much rather be a month late than a month early. Job one is still finishing the 737-7, the 737-10 and the 777X, and getting our balance sheet back to solidly investment grade. We will do a new airplane when the market, the technology and we are ready, and it has to be 20% to 30% better than what flies today. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. The financials will follow our production performance.

rolls_royce.public_statement: Rolls-Royce is launching the UltraFan narrowbody engine this year. We don't commit that easily. Until we are sure we will deliver, we don't commit, and when we commit, we deliver. UltraFan has run at full power. It scales from widebody down to narrowbody, and it is about 10% better than the best engine flying today. With fuel where it is, that efficiency is worth more to every airline. Boeing has told the industry what its next single-aisle needs: an engine launched by 2031 and ready by 2038. Ours is launched in 2031 and will be ready in 2038, on a proper testing schedule, with the support around it in place before it enters service. Narrowbody is a duopoly today, and we are probably the only one who can go in. We are not after market share. We are after high-quality, sustainable profit and cash, and the right reward for the risks we take, so our terms are standard. Today's financials are today's financials; I worry about tomorrow's financials. Widebody remains the heart of Rolls-Royce, and the Trent 1000 investment is putting more time on wing on the 787. This is a milestone on our journey, not our final destination.

airbus.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. With fuel prices high, our customers need the most efficient aircraft, and renewing fleets is the fastest lever they have on both cost and decarbonisation. Our next-generation single-aisle is in full development and remains on track to enter service in the 2035-2037 window. Until then, the A320 Family remains the backbone of our customers' fleets, and our production ramp-up stays disciplined and controlled. On widebodies, we are taking the next step for the A350 Family: a new engine option, timed so that it starts once our single-aisle development peak is behind us. We will not stretch our engineering teams across two development programmes while castings, forgings and skilled labour stay tight. Rolls-Royce has been our widebody partner for decades, and we have asked it to bring its next generation of engine technology to this aircraft. We continue to recruit the engineers and technicians the Airbus of the 30s needs, in Europe and at our sites around the world. These are disciplined investments, made with a commitment to shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility. We will keep working for a tariff-free, level playing field in aerospace.

rolls_royce.public_statement: Rolls-Royce is stopping the UltraFan narrowbody programme. In 2031 we said we would stop it if the next Boeing single-aisle went to another engine. Both new single-aisles now fly the LEAP derivative, so that is what we are doing. We don't commit that easily, and when we commit, we deliver. That includes the commitment to stop. I don't like options management in business: once you make a choice, that activity is gone. The money we have spent is sunk; the technology is not. UltraFan's geared architecture, its gearbox and its materials go into our widebody engines and into today's fleet, to put more time on wing. Widebody is the heart of Rolls-Royce. Long-haul traffic is coming back faster than anyone forecast, and we will support every Trent XWB, Trent 7000 and Trent 1000 operator for the life of their fleets. We are not after market share. We are after high-quality, sustainable profit and cash, and the right reward for the risks we take. Today's financials are today's financials. I worry about tomorrow's financials. This is a milestone on our journey, not our final destination.

ROUND 3 (2036-2045), the final round. Team: faury-toepfer-wagner-2026. Inject: widebody demand boom (+15% widebody demand to the end of the game). Our levers this round are limited to cancelling the A350 Re-engine, Delay Tactics and Poaching. There is no launch lever, because NGSA and the A350 Re-engine have both launched.

SITUATION (brief)
- NGSA: launched 2028, in service since 2035 on the CFM LEAP derivative (UltraFan requested, then fell back).
- A350 Re-engine: launched 2035, in development, flying the GE GEnx upgrade (UltraFan widebody requested, then fell back). Planned EIS 2040.
- Boeing fps: Solo, 10-year ramp-up, launched 2031, on the CFM LEAP derivative (GTF2 requested; Pratt & Whitney cancelled it). EIS 2038, in development.
- Boeing 737 Rate Increase: committed in 2031.
- No 787 Re-engine.
- Delay Tactics: never used, not exposed.
- Engine makers: Rolls-Royce UltraFan narrowbody launched 2031 (ready 2038) with no airframe; GEnx package committed; CFM has offered RISE for a 2036-37 airframe. whatif shows that none of their possible round-3 moves changes our PV or metrics: Rolls-Royce uf_wb in 2036, Rolls-Royce cancelling uf_nb, CFM open fan in 2036 and CFM lobbying all leave us at 36.451. Our engines are locked.

TRIGGERS (profile s5)
- Rows 1-2: fps launched late. NGSA already leads (2035 against 2038), so no programme change [A-0246, A-0110, A-0409].
- Row 7: the Rate Increase is committed. No programme change; Poaching only while a programme is in development [A-0019, A-0159, A-0218].
- Row 12: engine fallbacks. Never cancel over them [A-0218, A-0125, A-0360].
- Row 5: no 787 Re-engine, so the A350 Re-engine stands. Cancel only if a 787 Re-engine enters service first and loses at least $1B [A-0364, A-0090].
- Widebody boom: no row covers it. The closest precedent is the A350F entering the large-freighter market with "the airframe they know" [A-0255, A-0327, A-0160], and the A330neo sold on price and availability against a newer Boeing product [A-0090, A-0091]. Reading: keep and exploit the widebody derivative; no new widebody spend.
- Row 10 / MAX-grounding precedent: take share through deliveries and contracts, not tactics [A-0158, A-0163, A-0165].

FINANCE TEAM (options --compact and whatif on wg5-2045; $B Airbus dPV)
Stage game:
- A1 no move 36.382; A2 Poaching 36.451; A3 Delay Tactics 37.099; A4 Delay Tactics + Poaching 37.168.
- A5-A8 cancel rea350: 33.165 / 33.05 / 33.882 / 33.766.
- Pure Nash: B1 (Boeing no new move) x A4. Boeing's best response to every non-cancel option is B1.

Matrix (Airbus PV for none / Poaching / Delay Tactics / Delay Tactics + Poaching; Boeing PV is our estimate):
- Boeing idle: 36.382 / 36.451 / 37.099 / 37.168 (Boeing 4.207 / 3.931 / 0.143 / -0.133).
- 787 Re-engine 2036: 33.271 / 33.341 / 33.988 / 34.058 (Boeing 1.445 at most).
- 787 Re-engine 2038: 33.819 / 33.888 / 34.536 / 34.605.
- 787 Re-engine 2040: 34.297 / 34.366 / 35.013 / 35.083.
- 787 Re-engine 2042: 34.712 / 34.781 / 35.429 / 35.498.
- Cancel fps: 47.546 / 47.616 / 47.314 / 47.384.
- 787 Re-engine 2036 + cancel fps: 44.436 / 44.505 / 44.204 / 44.273.

Increments:
- Delay Tactics adds +0.70 to +0.72 wherever fps continues, and -0.23 if Boeing cancels fps.
- Poaching adds +0.069 to +0.070 in every case.
- Keeping the A350 Re-engine is worth +3.22 with Boeing idle (36.382 against 33.165) and +0.52 even against a 787 Re-engine in 2036 (33.271 against 32.756).
- Every 787 Re-engine year lowers Boeing's own estimated PV (4.207 down to 1.4-3.1).

RED-LINE AND DOCTRINE FILTER
- Cancelling rea350: fails the s6 cancel rule (no 787 Re-engine in service first) and costs -3.22.
- Delay Tactics: passes hard rule 4. It would be the first and only round, against an fps in development, with no exposure possible in the last round. It fails the s6 test (+0.72 < $1B) and the team's stricter test: it does not change who enters service first, since NGSA 2035 leads fps 2038, or 2039 with Delay Tactics. Under the team decision rule a failed test is a soft veto, overridable only with at least $1B over the best passing option (+0.717 < 1.0). Profile s9 step 6 also prefers the default (off) when it is within $1B. Survivors: A1 and A2.

EXCO DELIBERATION
FAURY (frames; medium confidence, incentives high):
- Five pillars first [AX-0073, AX-0081; A-0331]. Delay Tactics is the covert lever the integrity pillar argues against [A-0474, A-0478]. It would be a Board "abnormal risk" item [AX-0026; A-0298, A-0299], and at +0.72 it changes no entry-into-service order.
- The Airbus of the 30s is delivered: NGSA in service on our own clock, EIS 2035 [AX-0020].
- Proposal: the s11.2 round-3 default. Hold both programmes, take share through deliveries in the replacement wave, keep the A350 Re-engine for the widebody recovery [AX-0019, AX-0083], and run Poaching while it is in development.
TOEPFER (cash test; low confidence, role-derived):
- NGSA capex ended in 2034. Round-3 cash is the A350 Re-engine at $4.2B/5 = $0.84B a year (2035-39), plus $0.25B Poaching in 2036: a peak of about $1.1B, far inside one year's FCF (EUR 4.75bn, about $5.2B) [AX-0104].
- Net cash is preserved [AX-0102, AX-0022]. No overlap, no strain.
- Robustness: the plan's worst case is +33.341 (787 Re-engine 2036), positive.
- Cancelling rea350 destroys $3.2B against the remaining spend, which fails his payback test [A-0364]. PASS for A2.
WAGNER (production test; very low confidence, role-derived):
- No new concurrency under the standing supply crunch [AX-0054, AX-0060].
- The ramp priority is NGSA rate through the 2037-2046 wave, with rate producibility as the gate [A-0441, A-0303].
- The A350 Re-engine on GEnx has eis_add 0 and no wait; the engine fallback is no reason to cancel (row 12).
- Delay Tactics adds supplier-relationship risk in a crunch where we are buying, not blocking, capacity [A-0457, A-0317]. PASS for A2.
DECISION (team rule):
- The highest-PV survivor is A2 (Poaching): 36.451 against Boeing idle, Boeing's best response.
- No override is used, so the game ends with no override spent.

BOARD GATE
- No Board item this round: no launch, no cancellation, no Delay Tactics.
- Poaching is ExCo level ($0.25B, below EUR 300m). It is public and presented as recruitment for the Airbus of the 30s [A-0366, A-0485, A-0330, A-0339]. Hard rule 5 is met because the A350 Re-engine is in development until 2040.

PREMIUMS
- Doctrine premium: $0.72B (A4 37.168 against A2 36.451 with Boeing idle; $0.70-0.72B against any 787 Re-engine year; it turns to +$0.23B in our favour if Boeing cancels fps). Accepted under s6/s9 step 6, within the $1B epsilon.
- Historical reason: Airbus is a post-DPA company with integrity as its first paid objective [A-0474, A-0331, AX-0073]. There is no record of it obstructing a rival's supplier (profile s10). In the MAX grounding it won share by delivering and holding customers to contract [A-0158, A-0165].
- Objective premium: $0. The only repair would add PV; it is blocked by doctrine tests, not by price.

OBJECTIVES (per-round check, five-player)
- Before (no Airbus orders, public moves only):
  - nb_share_60 MISSED by -0.22 (59.78% in 2040/2045/2050). The 2031 Rate Increase takes 2035 to 58.0%, and NGSA's lead over the fps recovers 1.78pp in 2036-38.
  - protect_a320 MET at 0.0 (only 2030 counts, at 60.0%).
- After (Poaching): unchanged. nb_share_60 MISSED -0.22; protect_a320 MET 0.0.
- Engine requested rr_ultrafan_nb, flown cfm_leap_plus. It is locked, so the committed and fallback states coincide; supplier moves change nothing.
- Threat cases this round:
  - 787 Re-engine (any year): metrics unchanged (widebody only).
  - Boeing cancels fps: nb_share_60 MET at +1.47.
- Repair tested: one round of Delay Tactics slips the fps to 2039 and gives nb_share_60 MET at +0.58 (60.58%), worth +0.717. It is blocked by the s6 $1B test and the team's who-enters-first test. objectives.md s7 anticipated this ("No case tested reached $1B... expect to log the miss").
- Blocking rule: s6 Delay Tactics test plus the team's stricter Delay Tactics rule. Not a hard red line.
- Final position: nb_share_60 is not attainable within doctrine (gap -0.22pp); protect_a320 is met. Best attainable position: both programmes held, NGSA leading the wave, and A350 Re-engine widebody share rising to 46.05% in 2045 and 50.9% in 2050.

PREDICTION BASIS (Boeing)
- No launch and no cancellation (about 70%).
- A 787 Re-engine lowers Boeing's PV in every year we tested (best 3.13 against 4.21 idle). Boeing said it would "not run a second major development on top of" fps. Cancelling fps is -17.
- The widebody boom raises the odds of a 787 Re-engine, especially from 2038 once fps development ends: about 25%.
- The Rate Increase is already committed and not available again.

EXPECTED dPV: 0.70 x 36.451 + 0.25 x ~34.1 (787 Re-engine 2038-40 weighted) + 0.03 x 47.616 + 0.02 x 44.505, about 36.4.

Evidence followed: A-0019, A-0090, A-0091, A-0110, A-0125, A-0158, A-0159, A-0160, A-0163, A-0165, A-0218, A-0246, A-0255, A-0298, A-0299, A-0303, A-0317, A-0327, A-0330, A-0331, A-0339, A-0360, A-0364, A-0366, A-0409, A-0441, A-0457, A-0474, A-0478, A-0485; AX-0019, AX-0020, AX-0022, AX-0026, AX-0054, AX-0060, AX-0073, AX-0081, AX-0083, AX-0102, AX-0104. disclose: NGSA entered service in 2035 on the CFM LEAP-derived engine, an engine family our A320neo customers already fly. It is ramping through the replacement wave alongside the A320neo Family. There is no change to the programme.

The A350 Re-engine (GE GEnx upgrade) is in development for entry into service around 2040. Airbus is neither changing nor cancelling it. With long-haul demand recovering, the A350 Family will compete for every widebody campaign.

CFO: NGSA development spend is complete. The A350 Re-engine and our recruitment are funded from operating cash flow, and peak annual programme spend stays well below one year's free cash flow. Our commitment to shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility, our net cash position and our dividend policy are unchanged.

rounds.market_narrative: With NGSA in service on time and the engine field closed, single-aisle buyers stop waiting. Rolls-Royce's UltraFan narrowbody exit leaves both new airframes on the LEAP derivative. A320neo lessors firm NGSA slots for the replacement wave, though GTF operators get no common engine. Boeing's fps disclosure now matches the record, and LEAP-1B commonality brings 737 MAX customers back. But they want 2038 flown first, while Airbus keeps hiring Boeing engineers. CFM/GE ties RISE to a committed airframe, so buyers see no open-fan leapfrog before the mid-2040s. In the long-haul boom, 787 customers queue for slots. With no UltraFan widebody coming, Trent XWB fleets accept the GEnx-powered A350 Re-engine.
